body: Artist Kurd Alsleben in collaboration with physicist Cord Passow used an analogue computer (EAI 231 R) in Hamburg to create parametric generative art. The analog computer, combined with a mechanical drawing mechanism, produced graphical works of waves and lines based on the changing results of an equation. By adjusting the parameters of the equation, the outputs varied in visual form.

Karl Götz’s Statistisch-metrische Modulation (Statistical-metrical Modulation) is a series of hand-drawn Raster Pictures of 2 x 2 cm black and white squares on pieces of variously-sized cardboard. Götz was fascinated by the dematerialization of the art object that computers were enabling. He believed this was a paradigm shift. Statistisch-metrische Modulation was an attempt to explore this digital aesthetic (manually) before it was possible electronically. But Götz could clearly see what was coming: “When one thinks how much ‘easier,’ or less taxing, it would be to realize such [raster] pictures electronically, that is to say, that they would appear on the screen. It is obvious that these technical means will be used”(1963).

body: John Whitney Sr., pioneer in the field of computer-generated art and animation, founded Motion Graphics Incorporated. It became one of the first companies to use computers for creating graphics and animation. Whitney’s work and innovations would normalize the use of computers in the creative arts and had a profound impact on the development of computer generated images. The work at Motion Graphics was largely completed by a mechanical analog computer built by Whitney himself that controlled cameras above the artwork, a technique he used for the film Vertigo in 1958. He used this invention to create other film and television title sequences and commercials. While mechanical, Whitney’s machines anticipated future computer software.

body: Playing a significant role in the development of Kinetic and Op Art, the Parisian collective aimed to explore the relationship between art, science and technology to create works that empirically engaged with new materials and challenged traditional notions of art.
The fusion of science and art would be a pivotal feature of computer art as well as digital generative art.

Founded by Hector García Miranda, Horacio García Rossi, Hugo Demarco, Julio Le Parc, Vera Molnár, François Molnár, François Morellet, Sergio Moyano, Servanes (Simone Revoil), Joël Stein, Francisco Sobrino, and Yvaral (Jean-Pierre Vasarely), Centre de Recherche d’Art Visuel was “a center for visual research where the artists could work together towards the realization of their common formal and theoretical goals.
In the summer of 1960, the young artists rented a small garage in the Marais district of Paris, which provided them with a common meeting and exhibition space.”

The group would change its name to Groupe de Recherche d’Art Visuel (GRAV) in July 1961. GRAV artists used light, motion and other perceptual elements to create immersive and interactive artworks that required the viewer’s participation. These would all be crucial concepts to the development of electronic art.

Their work explicitly built upon the ideas of Victor Vasarely’s Yellow Manifesto., while implicitly building upon previous, even more radical movements such as Gutai in Japan and Allan Kaprow’s happenings in New York.

Further, Vera Molnar’s time as a member of GRAV was instrumental in shaping her approach to art. While she was initially focused on traditional forms of art such as painting and drawing, her time with GRAV exposed her to new techniques and approaches to art-making.

Through her involvement with the group, Molnar became interested in exploring the relationship between art and technology, which would lead her later in the decade to experiment with computer-generated images. She began creating algorithmic art using early computer programming languages such as FORTRAN. Although she had a disposition toward abstraction since childhood, her work became increasingly focused on the use of geometry and pattern.

Molnar’s time with GRAV also had an impact on her aesthetic sensibilities, influencing her interest in the use of repetitive forms, simple shapes and bold colors. She continued to explore these themes in her later computer-generated artworks, creating intricate and mesmerizing geometric patterns that play with the viewer’s perception, beginning in 1968.

Overall, Molnar’s time with GRAV helped to shape her approach to art and technology, which along with her concept of the “Machine Imaginaire” (Imaginary Computer) led to her becoming one of the great pioneers of computer-generated art.
From the Bright Moments Buenos Aires Timeline Poster:

Argentine painters Horacio García Rossi and Julio Le Parc, alongside luminaries like François Morellet and Vera Molnár, founded the Centre de Recherche d’Art Visuel, renamed GRAV in 1961, the profoundly important collective that helped bridge the analog and digital art worlds as part of the New Tendencies movement. Initially, the group was rooted in op and kinetic art, two critical predecessors of electronic art. Like Mac Entyre’s Pintura Generativa, the group aimed to liberate art from the static canvas.
The first commercially issued recording of computer generated music, Music from Mathematics (full album), created by John R. Pierce and Max Mathews at Bell Labs.
This work is not only some of the earliest digital electronic music ever produced, it also some of the earliest digital generative art and digital art, generally.
According to the New York Times:

“While not the first person to make sound with a computer, Max was the first one to do so with a replicable combination of hardware and software that allowed the user to specify what tones he wanted to hear.”

The Times article goes on to add how Mathews’s early attempts to create computer-generated music, “laid the groundwork for a revolutionary advancement in music, the reverberations of which are felt everywhere today.”

Perhaps most interesting for our story, one such piece, Effet esthétique de l’inversion des fonctions par la fluctuation de l’attention, appeared at this incredibly prestigious, landmark exhibition by a relatively unkown thirty-six year old Hungarian artist, Vera Molnár.

body: At the Wichita Branch of the Military Aircraft Systems Division of Boeing, William Fetter coined the term “computer graphics” to refer to his plotter drawings. He created visualization on a computer “to help airplane designers and engineers envision on a computer screen the diverse human body shapes and a pilot’s limited vision in a cockpit as a plane lands.” These were among the first true perspective drawings produced by a computer. These historic artifacts are some of the beginnings of the computer graphics industry and would later in the ’60s be displayed as Boeing Man.

body: John McCarthy at MIT introduced the programming language LISP (List Processing) in 1960. He published the language in his seminal paper in on recursive functions in programming. LISP would go on to be used in Symbolics graphics computer. Nearly twenty years later, Peter Beyls would use LISP to create some of his early computer-generated work. Harold Cohen would also use LISP in his work with AARON. LISP thus significantly influenced digital art by introducing a programming environment conducive to creative expression and generative processes. LISP’s unique symbolic manipulation capabilities enabled artists to more easily represent artistic concepts as code. Along with John Backus’s FORTRAN (1957) and John G. Kemeny and Thomas E. Kurtz’s BASIC (1964), LISP was one of the most significant early digital software developments in programmed art.

body: This convention-defying work of chance art saw Saint Phalle create an assemblage of white, found objects, surrounded by sacks of colored paint. She would then fire a rifle at the paint sacks to explosively create the work. A fascinating example of the ingenuity and breadth of generative art, the rifle plays a decisive role in the system that ultimately creates the art and could thus be considered an autonomous system.

body: Steinbuch’s books introduced the concept of “information processing” as a core function of machines and computers. This idea laid the foundation for the development of artificial intelligence and cognitive science. According to Gottfried Jäger, the book “was seminal for my way of thinking.” The book attempted to explain intellectual functions in terms of information transfers and science. Automat und Mensch taught Jäger that “a human brain and a hand weren’t necessary anymore for artistic expression. It could be also a technical apparatus. A camera or a computer were capable of achieving intellectual results.” Thus, the book significantly influenced the way we understand the relationship between humans and machines. Steinbuch’s work helped to shape the field of cybernetics and inspired further research in the field of computer science, leading to the upcoming digital revolution in art.

body: The Lithuanian-American artist and curator, Maciunas founded and organized the Fluxus (“flowing” in English) movement’s first event. The event, which would be the first of a brilliant, art-chaning series, included readings by poet Frank Kuenstler. Fluxus, an international avant-garde movement, rejected traditional artistic mediums and emphasized performance, humor and experimentation. The movement has strong ties to Dada’s anti-art sentiment and is considered to be part of a broader Neo-Dada movement that emerged around this time. Fluxus has strong ties to both computer and generative art, particularly regarding the dematerialization of art and the rise of conceptual art which the movement propels. Fluxus also often features elements of rules-based practice. Additionally, it is multi-disciplinary with collaboration and audience participation encouraged, two further hallmarks of the rise of electronic art. Chance and randomness also play an important role in Fluxus performances. The focus was on process and concept rather than a unified finished art object, a tradition that continues today in many circles of digital generative art, particularly within academia. Like GRAV, Fluxus artists sought to diminish distinctions between art and everyday life with Deleuzian work often incorporating non-traditional materials and methods.

body: Dissatisfied with 1960 Venice Biennale, Brazilian artist Almir Mavignier and art critic Matko Meštrović sought to organize a new exhibition that showcased “new tendencies” in art not yet supported by the establishment. The exhibition was held at the Gallery for Contemporary Art, Zagreb. The New Tendencies movement was hugely important for the development of computer and digital art. Technology was central to the movement’s goals: “Many followers of the NT [New Tendencies] have tried to give their work the habit of the machine or else they have based their procedures on the use of mechanical or electrical devices; they have all dreamt of the machines—and now the machines have arrived,” said critic Radoslav Putar. Nove tendencije, the exhibition, featured work of Concrete Art that blurred the lines between painting and sculpture. GRAV member François Morellet’s work was described as “programmed painting.” Artists from the Zero Group also presented work in their Lumino-Kinetic style. These exhibitions and groups serve as the extension in the genealogy of generative art of the lumino-kinetic tradition, which leads ultimately later in the decade to the development of electronic art.

body: Presented for the first time at the Hanover Fair, this revolutionary drawing machine would be used by early computer pioneers such as Georg Nees and Frieder Nake. Designed by the prolific German engineer Konrad Zuse, the Z 64 was one of the first computer-driven plotters, allowing artists to create precise geometric shapes and patterns on paper, translated from computer code. The Graphomat Z 64 was particularly important for computer art because it allowed artists to create complex and precise works without the need for manual labor. This made it possible to create large-scale works that would have been impossible with traditional artistic methods. The Graphomat Z 64 helped to pave the way for the development of computer art and inspired a generation of artists to explore new forms of digital expression, enabled by the Graphomat.

body: An Approach to Cybernetics by Gordon Pask is a foundational text in the field of cybernetics, which explores the principles of information and control in complex systems. Pask presents the concept of “learning machines” in the book. These are machines capable of acquiring knowledge and modifying their behavior based on that knowledge, similar to a pupil-teacher relationship. Pask argues that these machines should not be designed as fixed, predetermined systems, but rather should be allowed to learn and adapt in response to feedback from their environment. The book also covers the main areas of cybernetics such as feedback, communication, and learning, and argues that these concepts are fundamental to understanding both natural and artificial systems. The book is based on Pask’s own experience designing the responsive machines he describes, such as the Musicolour (1953–57).

body: This work by a key member of the Japanese Gutai movement serves as an example of their groundbreaking use of chance. Shiraga swung, slipped and spun back and forth from a rope attached to the ceiling with wet oil paint on his feet. As he swung, his feet would come in contact with the canvas on the floor, creating the piece. This could be considered a work of material generative art with the rope-swing-body-paint-motion combination forming the autonomous system.

body: The First Computer Art

Experimenting on the side with computer-generated creative expression while at Bell Labs, Noll avoided calling the works he documented and produced “art.” He referred to them instead as “patterns” in order to avoid controversy. Patterns by 7090, as Noll named them, are among the first known algorithmically generated art on a digital computer.
These are among the first-known digital generative graphics.
These were programmed on FORTRAN with an IBM 7090 mainframe computer. Noll printed the patterns on a Stromberg-Carlson 4020 Microfilm Printer.
In a 1962 Technical Memorandum describing the process and showcasing the pieces, Noll coined the term “programmer-artist.”
In the Technical Memorandum, Noll speculated that with greater study, “the programmer-artist might be better prepared to produce not just haphazard patterns, but ‘true art.’”
Thus, these experiments paved the way for further exploration, particularly at Bell Labs.
Noll would go on to display the work publicly three years later, at the Howard Wise Gallery in April 1965.

Programmed art extended the aesthetics and concepts of Constructivism and Neo-Plasticism. According to Grant Taylor, “computer art appealed to the same concepts of objectivity and the will to detach the art object from the idea.” This work thus played an important in calling for the dematerialization of art, which was a profound leap that art undertook, in this time period.

body: With no prior personal relationships and independently from one another, American Pop Art exploded in 1962 with four monumental exhibitions. Roy Lichtenstein had his first show of paintings based on comic-book panels at the Castelli Gallery (New York City) in February. Andy Warhol had his first solo Pop art show, 32 Campbell’s Soup Cans at the Ferus Gallery (Los Angeles) in July. James Rosenquist had his first solo show at the Green Gallery (New York City). Lichtenstein, Warhol, Ed Ruscha and Wayne Thiebaud opened the group exhibition New Painting of Common Objects at the Pasadena Art Museum in September. Pop Art played an important role in the development of digital generative art with its emphasis on collaboration, process and mass production. Warhol’s prints also have much in common with digital generative art collections with a unified theme but individual random variation. Casey Reas has spoken of the importance of the mass production of art as a prerequisite for NFTs. This is a monumental step in that direction.

body: In this seminal report for the Air Force Office of Scientific Research, Engelbart proposed the idea of using technology to enhance human cognitive abilities. He argued that by developing tools that amplified human intelligence, we could better address complex social and environmental problems, creating a more equitable and sustainable world. His ideas were influential in the development of modern computing, user interface design and collaborative work systems. This vision of the computer as a tool for enhancing human intellect would be echoed by Vera Molnár in her views that the computer enhanced human intuition.

body: In the catalogue for this early GRAV exhibition, Morellet would spell out the group’s relevance to the programmed, digital generative art of today.

Morellet wrote of the ability of “programmed experimental painting,” essentially today’s digital generative art, to be used in order to experimentally “demystify art.” He believed that generative techniques could produce thousands of works of art at a time for aesthetic experiments.

Morellet was proposing a new science of art that he hoped could reveal insights into questions of aesthetics. To conduct his aesthetic experiments, he produced a multitude of works following a program. He called this early material generative art, “programmed experimental painting.”

By producing many generative iterations, Morellet sought to gain more data points for his scientific investigation into aesthetics. He aimed to satisfy “the need on the part of a section of the public who wants to share in the “creation” of works of art, and who are interested in demystifying art and in better understanding it.”
In other words, Morellet used generative techniques as a tool to better understand art’s underlying aesthetic concepts.

body: “’Concept art’ is first of all an art of which the material is ‘concepts.’” -Henry Flynt in “Concept Art” Flynt, an American philosopher, musician and artist, coined the term “concept art” in his 1961 essay “Concept Art”, published in An Anthology in 1963. In the essay, Flynt argues that art should be based on ideas rather than aesthetics. He claims that artists should focus on creating thought-provoking works rather than visually appealing ones, a key tenet of post-modernism. Conceptual art shares generative art’s interest in the process of creation, as the term “concept art” was later adopted by other artists, including Sol LeWitt, a progenitor of material generative practices. In many ways, computer art specifically can be seen as an extension of conceptual art, according to Frank Popper and Grant Taylor. In addition to aesthetic overlap, both movements emphasize the importance of ideas over materials and use can use algorithmic procedure, text, and other non-traditional mediums to convey their ideas. Conceptual artists like Sol LeWitt produced instructions for other humans to carry out. Computer artists like Manfred Mohr produced algorithms for a computer plotter to carry out. This was another hugely important step in the dematerialization of art.

cite.label: Taylor, Grant D. When the Machine Made Art: The Troubled History of Computer Art, 48. New York: Bloomsbury Academic, 2014.

body: These objects are some of the first creative computer-generated imagery along with A. Michael Noll’s Patterns by 7090 from a year earlier in 1962.

They may, however, be the first objects created with the intention of being fine art by a digital computer. Noll considered his work “patterns” at the time to avoid scrutiny. But as of 2023 in a conversation with me, he declared Patterns by 7090 to certainly be works of art. We will share this conversation with Dr. Noll soon.
Splatter Pattern won first prize and Stained Glass Window second in the Computers and Automation computer art contest of 1963, both plotted on an Electronic Associates DATA PLOTTER.

The United States Army Ballistic Research Laboratories (BRL) was a scientific research institution established in 1938, primarily focused on the development of ballistic technology for the U.S. military.
During and after WWII, it would also be a key contributor to the computing revolution.

In the 1960s, the BRL became involved in the development of computer graphics and, thus, digital art, with its attempts to visualize missile trajectories. The creations were produced just one year after the Cuban Missile Crisis.

One of the BRL’s contributions to the field of computer art was the creation of the “splatter pattern” technique. This technique involved using a computer program to randomly generate patterns of dots and lines, which were then printed out on a large format plotter.

It’s telling that some of the first machines capable of creating digital computer art were used to do so. BRL not only helped to establish computer-generated images as a viable form of artistic expression, it also paved the way for the development of the computer, computer graphics and animation.

body: “Computer art” is born! The trade journal Computers and Automation significantly impacted the infancy of computer art. The magazine was the first to use the phrase “computer art,” which it used on the title page of the January 1963 edition. This would help to popularize the term as well as the movement for another decade. Crucially, it also started the pivotal “Computer Art Contest.” The contest helped to popularize the concept of using computers as a tool for artistic expression. The magazine also provided a forum for artists and technologists to exchange ideas and discuss the potential of computer art. Computers and Automation helped to establish a community of artists and technologists who were interested in exploring the creative potential of the computer. It providing the foundation for the movement in the coming years.

body: Condensation Cube (1963–65) is a sealed transparent acrylic cube containing a small quantity of water. The temperature differential between the inside of the cube and the room causes water vapour to condense and run down the inside walls in continually changing patterns. The rate of condensation and evaporation is affected by the temperature and humidity of the environment, resulting in an ever-changing and unpredictable pattern of water droplets. The work emphasizes the role of natural processes and chance in the creation of art, demonstrating the potential of generative art to create dynamic and evolving artworks beyond the digital realm. It is also a key example of material generative art. While a canonical example of material generative art, the piece does highlight the at-times lacking conceptual foundation of some generative practices.

body: One of the most iconic works of early computer art, Noll’s Gaussian Quadratic is a computer-generated artwork consisting of a series of connected lines generated by mathematical algorithms, Noll created while working at Bell Labs.

The piece was one of the first artworks to be created entirely by a computer, demonstrating the potential of computers as a tool for artistic expression and inspiring future generations of artists to experiment with computer-generated imagery.
Noll himself describes it:

“Ninety-nine lines connect 100 points whose horizontal coordinates are Gaussian. Vertical coordinates increase according to a quadratic equation. As a point reaches the top, it is reflected to the bottom to continue its rise. The exact proportions of this pattern were chosen from many other examples. This particular proportion is vaguely similar to the painting Ma Jolie by Picasso.”

Derived from Noll’s 1962 experiments, the piece today is in the collection of the V&A Museum as well as Spalter Digital. The piece would go on to be displayed at the first public exhibition of computer art in the United States, at New York’s Howard Wise Gallery in 1965 as well as Cybernetic Serendipity (1968).

It was created by kinetic light artist Thomas Wilfred who pioneered the “lumia” art form in the 1920s. The extremely complex work was created on a device consisting of metal, fans, electric motors and light.

body: 1963 marks the year that Nake, the computer art pioneer, began making computer art.
His compArt ER56 series refers to the program created to produce his work from 1963 to 1965.

Random Polygon Move, the earliest catalogued example dating from July 1964, is an early plotter drawing similar in style to Noll’s Gaussian Quadratic with lines connecting points determined by a random number generator.

body: Paik’s first exhibit, at Galerie Parnass in Wuppertal in March 1963, marked the birth of video art and represented turning point in the dematerialization of art. The pioneering Korean artist, then working in Germany, transformed thirteen televisions into a multimedia installation that incorporated music, moving images and electronic sound. He combined technology and art in a novel way, using television sets as a canvas to create a new medium of artistic expression, helping to free art from the confines of the static canvas and anticipating much of today’s animated art. Paik’s work showed how technology could be used to create art accessible to the masses through the use of electronic media. It was thus an important example of both mass-media art and the dematerialization of art, two of Casey Reas’s preconditions for NFTs.

Zajac’s Gyro Gravity Gradient Attitude Control System is a study of satellite motion, showing how one could always have a side facing earth during orbit. Zajac programmed the frames in Fortran on an IBM 7090, the same Device A. Michael Noll used to produce his early plotted works.

body: ASCII (American Standard Code for Information Interchange) was adopted as a standard in 1963. This code is a character encoding system that assigns unique numbers to represent each letter and character of the alphabet. ASCII has played a significant role in both computer and digital art. In computer art, ASCII characters have been used to create images, designs, and animations, with artists utilizing the unique visual properties of ASCII characters to create often abstract works. Well known examples include Kenneth Knowlton and Leon Harmon’s Computer Nude (Studies in Perception I) (1966) and Vuk Ćosić’s Deep ASCII (1998). In digital art, ASCII has been used as a tool for text-based art with artists using characters to create intricate typographic compositions and designs. Overall, ASCII has provided artists with a powerful tool for creating digital works that are both visually unique and highly flexible. In terms of its importance at the time, ASCII allowed computers to communicate with each other in a standardized way, regardless of manufacturer or operating system. This meant that data could be easily transferred between different computers and devices, which helped to facilitate the growth of the digital age.

body: In his book Inventing the Future, Gabor discusses the role of science and technology in shaping the future of society. He argues that technological progress is essential for the advancement of civilization and that scientists and engineers have a responsibility to use their knowledge for the betterment of humanity. Gabor was a strong advocate for the use of technology in creative fields, believing that advancements in science and engineering had the potential to transform art and culture. His ideas helped shape the growing debate in society at the time about whether technology was a net positive or negative for humanity.

body: Ascott, British cybernetic and telematics arts pioneer, had his first exhibition at the Molton Gallery, London, in February 1963 with Diagram-boxes and Analogue Structures.
The exhibit itself featured “change-paintings and other works in wood, Perspex and glass.”
Ascott himself would say about the exhibition:

“My first London show at the Molton Gallery in 1964, Analogue Structures and Diagram Boxes, was the breakthrough exhibition, in which I exhibited work based on my enthusiasm for cybernetics that serves as the starting point of al my subsequent essays into interactivity, and my play with the metaphors of science.”
He has been asked which project in his career he wanted to be remembered by:

“It would be the Molton show, because it seeded ideas that have had legitimacy and relevance beyond the analogue structures I then employed, and informs the practice and theory of the ‘new media’ arts,” Ascot told Melentie Pandilovski.

body: Knowlton, a pioneer of computer art and animation, at Bell Labs developed BEFLIX, the first general-purpose programming language for computer animation.
BEFLIX is short for “Bell Flicks” and was written in macro FAP, the Fortran Assembly Program.
BEFLIX was used by artists, including Stan Vanderbeek to make some of the earliest experimental, abstract films in collaboration with Knowlton.

body: Doug Engelbart, a computer engineer, conceived the first computer mouse, which his engineer Bill English built from wood with one button. Engelbart’s invention was a significant contribution to the development of modern computing and the tools that would enable digital art. It revolutionized the way users interacted with computers, making it easier and more intuitive to navigate through graphical user interfaces.

He engaged with computer art on a philosophical level, believing artists created the “art computer” which had its own “artificial creativity.” He published his first computer-generated images in September 1964, going on to computer-generated literature and music.

Fetter had previously worked at Boeing to create some of the earliest computer graphics of a flight simulation in 1960. This 3D image of the human body with computer graphics was groundbreaking for its time and is still known famously as Boeing Man.

body: In 1964, the Molnárs planned and constructed their own three-story home and studio on Rue Hallé. Vera later reminisced, “It was the Morellets who lent us money, plus the family and the bank, which meant that we were poor all our lives.” Despite this, it was a spacious and comfortable dream home, profoundly influencing Vera’s artistic journey. Reflecting on the past, she marvels, “Did I already have a table? My own? Which wasn’t half for me, half a desk for François, where I could leave my stuff? There were things I couldn’t do [before] that time because I didn’t have a table.”

body: Arnold Rockman, art critic, and Leslie Mezei, computer scientist, together wrote: “the first recognizable piece of computer art criticism. Appearing in Canadian Art and entitled “The Electronic Computer as an Artist.” This seminal article possessed all of the basic elements of art criticism: historical context, stylistic analysis, and, most importantly, evaluative judgment,” according to Grant Taylor. Note from the title of the article, “The Electronic Computer as an Artist,” how even the earliest forms of computer art asked questions about authorship and the computer’s creative role.

body: Canadian Leslie Mezei, computer art pioneer and scholar, played a hugely important and influential role in the development of computer graphics. The lecture was held, according to Grant Taylor, “at the fourth meeting of the Computing and Data Processing Society of Canada.” Taylor continues, describing how Mezei spoke about “the possibility for formulating general laws of aesthetics that could aid in artistic design,” influeced by George David Birkhoff’s 1933 Aesthetic Measure. His interdisciplinary accomplishments cannot be overstated. In his own words: “In 1965 I became an Associate Professor of Computer Science at the University of Toronto. I taught the first Artificial Intelligence course in Canada in 1967, and in the same year, established the Computer Graphics Group, which became the Dynamic Graphics Project (DGP). [I had] an annual Bibliography from March 1967, and a regular column in ArtsCanada from April 1968 for two years. I started producing my own computer art in 1967, exploring geometric, mathematical and random transformations, and early representational images, using my SPARTA language, and animations with ARTA. They have been included in many exhibitions and published in many catalogues, articles and books.”

body: The first of Flavin’s homages to Vladimir Tatlin, co-founder of Constructivism, alludes to the Constructivist focus on modest industrial materials. Flavin’s modest industrial materials are, of course, fluorescent light tubes which he arranges to resemble Tatlin’s Tower. This never-built but highly influential structure was a monument to the ideals of the communist revolution. Flavin’s monument, in addition to materials, also pays homage to Tatlin’s futuristic, utopian ideals. This series demonstrates Constructivism’s influence on Minimalism, both of which were highly influential to digital generative art aesthetic.

body: Despite Victor Vasarely spawning the movement nearly a decade earlier with the manifesto and subsequent exhibition, Le Mouvement, the term “Op Art” was popularized in 1964 by Time Magazine, though its coinage is contested. Op Art and the related Kinetic Art were both focused on motion, perceived or real. Both precipitated the popularization of cybernetic art and the digital motion upcoming with computer-generated art. The culmination of the intersection between Op Art, cybernetic art and proto-digital art emerged at The Responsive Eye at MoMA the following year (1965).

Nees said after seeing this work plotted out by the Graphomat: “Here is something that will not vanish again. Look artists, one can make abstract art en masse! Why should an artist not let himself be helped by the computer?

body: The book that coined the phrase “the medium is the message,” Understand Media is a significant work in media theory and art history. The book expressed McLuhan’s highly influential ideas about media and its effects on human culture and behavior, still relevant today. McLuhan’s ideas would be further explored and greatly inspirational to artists in the second half of the ’60s that would begin experimenting with this new media technology (television, film, computers, audiotape, etc). This would include Robert Rauschenberg, Yvonne Rainer, John Cage, Andy Warhol, and Stan VanDerBeek who would collaborate with engineers from Bell Labs like Billy Klüver, later a founder of EAT. McLuhan argued that the medium through which information is conveyed shapes how people perceive and understand the world around them. It also popularized the idea of the global village. He introduced the concepts of “hot” and “cool” media, and how they influence people’s level of participation and engagement. His ideas also paved the way for later studies on the impact of technology on society, including the internet and of course art.

body: One of the computer art pioneer’s legendary pieces, Computer Composition with Lines won Computer and Automation’s first prize in 1965.

Most famously, Noll used the piece in his Mondrian experiment, seeking to pit a machine’s creative power against a human artist’s. He placed his own Computer Composition with Lines alongside Mondrian’s Composition with Lines and asked his colleagues which they preferred between the two. According to Noll himself:

“The conclusion of these investigations of computer-generated two-dimensional pictures is that the exciting potential of computers in art consists in their capability of producing mixtures of random elements with mathematically specified formulae for order.”

body: This 348-page tome by Max Bense, Aesthetica. Einführung in die neue Aesthetik, contained four volumes and a manifesto.

Bense published the four volumes between 1954 and 1960; the 1965 edition collects them and adds the manifesto. The works “anticipated the principles of computer art” and were foundational to the development of cybernetics.

Bense was one of the first theorists to recognize the potential of computer technology as a medium for art. In Aesthetica, he introduced the concept of “generative aesthetics,” and the ability to “program the beautiful” which emphasized the use of algorithms to create surprising and novel artistic forms.

This idea inspired artists and programmers to experiment with computer-generated art, leading to the birth of computer art as a distinct genre in the 1960s, where Bense’s impact was felt particularly in Europe at the University of Stuttgart with students Georg Nees and Frieder Nake, who would make some of the earliest computer art. Bense’s work helped establish the theoretical foundations for computer art and its potential as a medium for artistic expression.
From a previous entry on the importance of cybernetics:

Cybernetics would play a vital role in both the birth of digital art and artificial intelligence, thus making it one of the single most important moments on the timeline. Max Bense and his role at the University of Stuttgart explains the connection to computer art, specifically. He supervised Georg Nees’s doctorate and Frieder Nake sat in on his lectures, leaving an indelible marks on their thinking that last to this day, as this 2018 talk by Nake demonstrates.

For artificial intelligence, cybernetics was an early attempt to unite machines and organic beings in a functional way, as it sought a theory of control, feedback and communication applicable to machines as well as animals. In the book Art in the Age of Machine Learning, author Sofian Audry argues that the concept of machine learning dates back to cybernetics.

body: Opening 4 February and running from the 5th to the 19th, Computergrafik was the first of the three 1965 computer art exhibitions globally. Invited by Max Bense to show the graphical work Georg Nees had been working on, Computergrafik was held in the Studiengalerie of the Technische Hochschule Stuttgart. Nees was the only artist on display. The February exhibit was the first gallery exhibition of graphic works created by a digital computer, though a one-day showing of computer-generated images programmed by Joan Shogren at San Jose State College on 6 May 1963 preceded it. It opened just months before the Howard Wise show in New York (April). It would go on to greatly influence another exhibition several months later in November of the same year with Frieder Nake. The reaction from the general public and from the artistic community upon seeing the first computer art was negative and bordered on hostile.

body: On display in April 1965, the legendary Computer-Generated Pictures introduced computer art to the broader public, especially in the United States. The second of the three computer art exhibitions of 1965, Computer-Generated Pictures was the first in North America and the first held in a commercial gallery.

The show was held by artist-researchers A. Michael Noll and Béla Julesz spanning several years of their research from Bell Labs. Howard Wise was an industrialist and art lover, particularly Op and Lumino-Kinetic Art. An Op art lover, Wise was particularly interested in the pair’s work with 3D depth perception.

Julesz exhibited his random-dot stereograms, consisting of computer-generated patterns that gave the illusion of “binocular depth perception.” Today these are known as “magic eye” pictures. Meant to be viewed in 3D, they handed out glasses to visitors to view the works. The show featured Noll’s stereographic (3D) works as well (1964 link), along with his now legendary:
Patterns by 7090 Gaussian-Quadratic Computer Composition With Lines Vertical-Horizontal Number Three Ninety Parallel Sinusoids

Famously, not a single work sold; the public reception was cold to indifferent. The show was another example in art history of a visionary exhibition too far ahead of its time to be recognized or understood by contemporaries. Computer-Generated Pictures was a landmark development in the gradual acceptance of the computer’s role in art-making.

body: Opening November 5, 1965, computer grafik was Europe’s first computer art exhibition outside of a university and third ever public show. It was the third and final of the three famous 1965 shows.
Nake’s first ever exhibition, the show was highly influenced by the thinking of Max Bense and his views on generative aesthetics.
Nees took his doctorate under Bense, writing his thesis on computer art, and Nake sat in on Bense’s lectures.

The exhibition was extremely optimistic about the creative possibilities of computers and art. It asked questions about technology and art, as well as artificial intelligence, envisioning the out-sized creative possibilities that programmed art promised.
While some of these works actually sold for very small prices, public sentiment was muted at best.
This author, Peter Bauman spoke to Frieder Nake about the beginnings of computer art and more in “Frieder Nake on “Machinic” Miracles” at Le Random Editorials.

body: John Giorno’s Poetry Systems, “a nonprofit production company designed to introduce new, innovative poetry to wider audiences,” reflects Giorno’s belief that poetry, within the context of Pop-Art ideas, lagged behind other art forms in terms of media and inventiveness. He sought to innovate poetry by using modern communication technologies as a performance and publication space, leveraging telephones, televisions and records to connect with readers. Giorno would go on to collaborate with William Burroughs and Brion Gysin, among others.

body: The exhibition by William C. Seitz at The Museum of Modern Art ignited Opto-Kinetic Art and even inspired Vera Molnár shortly after.

This landmark exhibition of Op/Kinetic Art popularized the movements as well as the alliance between science, technology and art. The exhibition showcased some of the most influential artists of the twentieth-century, including Bridget Riley, Josef Albers, Ellsworth Kelly, Frank Stella and Victor Vasarely.

It also featured a large number of the newly dubbed “New Tendencies” movement which included Groupe de Recherche d’Art Visuel (GRAV). Computer art legend Vera Molnár was a member of GRAV as well as François Morellet. The exhibition emphasized the role of technology and movement in the creation of new forms of artistic expression. By linking Op Art and Kinetic Art together, the exhibition showed that art did not have to be a static image.

The Responsive Eye paved the way for innovative work that incorporated technology and science: namely, computer art and digital generative art. Three years later, Molnár would use a computer to create “Interruptions,” a work with a clear aesthetic nod to "The Responsive Eye.”
Casey Reas mentions The Responsive Eye to Le Random when discussing significant moments in generative art history.

body: One of the most cited and recognized works among the earliest computer art, Homage to Paul Klee (in English) draws inspiration from Klee’s Hauptweg und Nebenwege (1929) without Nake directly attempting to reproduce it algorithmically.

body: Hearing the words “five screens with computer” today, our minds automatically think of a laptop or desktop computer’s “screen” or digital display. As such screens did not exist in 1965, this piece’s “five screens” were actually “made of stainless steel, about thirty feet high, forty feet long and three feet deep,” according to Gustav Metzger himself in the Cybernetic Serendipity catalog. In this unrealized project, a computer would eject the screens’ elements one by one until the site was empty, a process that would take ten years. This “auto-destructive” art was a critique of the “rationalism” of computers and technology and backlash to their militaristic roots.

img.cap: Metzger’s model for Five Screens with Computer: five upright steel plates standing on a steel base, the maquette for the computer-controlled auto-destructive monument.
img.credit: Gustav Metzger, Five Screens with Computer, model, steel, 7.2 × 44.4 × 30.9 cm. © Generali Foundation Collection — Permanent Loan to the Museum der Moderne Salzburg. Photo: Werner Kaligofsky.

Pierce, the title refers to the James Joyce novel, alluding to the computer as a maturing artist. The article encouraged the use of artistic experimentation with computers and technology with a staunchly pro-technology argument.

body: This early Paik exhibit sought to establish the television as an artistic medium. Along with another of his exhibitions at Bonino (1968), these would establish the artist as a pioneer of video art. The exhibitions would also garner Paik critical attention, especially the piece Magnet TV, which featured a TV screen distorted by a large magnet, an example of material-digital generative art.

body: Exemplifying the influence of Kinetic Art on Op art, this motorized, kinetic structure demonstrates that Op Art did not have to solely rely on virtual movement. This also indicates the extent to which VIctor Vasarely’s ideas, particularly from his Yellow Manifesto, influenced Morellet.

body: Made by Noll at Bell Labs, this stereoscopic film of a “hypercube” is one of the earliest 3D computer graphic films.

Images were printed side-by-side, frame-by-frame and are meant for 3D freeviewing (like a “Magic Eye”). The work is similar to what Noll and Julesz exhibited at Howard Wise that year. The video can be viewed in the same way as a Magic Eye by relaxing the eye without the need for 3D glasses.
Listen to Peter Bauman’s interview with A. Michael Noll (transcript).

img.cap: Stills from A. Michael Noll’s Hypercube (1965), the computer-animated rotating four-dimensional hypercube, printed as paired left/right frames for stereoscopic free-viewing.

body: As Gutai gained fame in Europe, Jiro Yoshihara, accompanied by his son Michio, was invited to exhibit in Amsterdam. Only three-dimensional and new works were allowed with no paintings. Yoshihara presented nine previously well-received pieces and two new ones by Michio, impressing the audience and solidifying Gutai’s reputation outside of Japan as an exceptional avant-garde art group. This exhibition also featured new European avant-garde groups that had been inspired by the radical ideas of Gutai, including Nul and ZERO.

body: The article in which Knowlton explains BEFLIX and his early computer animation techniques, which he developed at Bell Labs.
Knowlton writes in the article:

“An automatic, electronic microfilm recorder can plot points and draw lines many orders of magnitude faster than a human draftsman can. This machine and the electronic computer which controls it promise to facilitate the production of animated movies for a wide range educational and research purposes.”
Listen to Peter Bauman’s interview with A. Michael Noll (transcript), where he discusses Knowlton, BEFLIX and the early days at Bell Labs.

img.credit: Kenneth C. Knowlton, A Computer Technique for the Production of Animated Movies, 1963, Bell Telephone Laboratories. Image: compArt database Digital Art (dada), University of Bremen.

body: This systems-based art exhibit would enable future digital generative practices. Curated by critic Lawrence Alloway, the exhibition coined the phrase “systemic painting” for systems-based work. Such work consisted of mostly abstract geometric compositions with repeated, organized patterns, rooted in minimalism. For Alloway, painting-as-a-system was when an artist created a collection of similar works based on simple rules. “The run of the image constitutes a system, with limits set up by the artist.” For systemic work, Alloway believed that “meaning is complete“ not after a single painting but only when viewing the entire collection as a whole. “The system is the means by which we approach the work of art.“ To analyze the system, “unity within variety" were also important. An example of the kind of system on display was the One Image, the recurring use of a single form. Examples included Kenneth Noland’s chevrons (below) and Ad Reinhardt’s crosses. 28 artists participated in the exhibition, including Agnes Martin (below), Ellsworth Kelly, Frank Stella and Jo Baer. The parallels are clear from this early exhibition of material generative art to today’s short and long form digital collections. “Systemic Painting” also profoundly influenced the aesthetics of artists beginning to create similar geometric compositions with computers.

img.cap: Installing Systemic Painting at the Solomon R. Guggenheim Museum, 1966: Lawrence Alloway oversees the hanging of Neil Williams’s Sartorial Habits of Billy Bo, with Frank Stella’s Wolfeboro IV at right.
img.credit: Solomon R. Guggenheim Museum Archives, New York, Exhibition files 189: Systemic Painting, A0003. © Solomon R. Guggenheim Foundation. Photographer not identified. Paintings by Neil Williams and Frank Stella. Image source.
img.alt: A team holds a large angular geometric painting against a gallery wall while Lawrence Alloway stands at right beside another shaped canvas.

body: Computer Technique Group, a Tokyo-based student collective, was founded in 1966. They would pioneer the concept of the artist-as-system-creator and are one of the most important groups in generative art history (digital or material).

This collective of art and engineering students, founded by Masao Kohmura and Haruki Tsuchiya, emphasized the role of the artistic expression in the group. The CTG manifesto explains how the group intended to function as not only a design office but also a think tank:

“CTG is an active think tank that takes advantage of well developed electronic computer systems and makes them serve the needs of human beings. We, the post-war generation, have been exploring our place in machine society for all our born days. Living without machines is attractive in its own way in our dreadful age but it is regressive evolution back towards apes, and is different from the creative evolution we are aiming for.

We will tame the computer’s appealing transcendental charm and restrain it from serving established power. This stance is the way to solve complicated problems in the machine society. We do not praise machine civilization, nor do we criticise it. By a strategic collaboration with artists, scientists and other creative people from a wide variety of backgrounds, we will deliberate carefully the relationships between human beings and machines, and how we should live in the computer age."

Besides these lofty ambitions, CTG would go on to introduce the concept of the artist as system creator. These systems could produce unlimited complex forms and patterns rather than just individual works, an immensely influential concept now ubiquitous in today’s generative art.
Image is copyrighted by The Artists and courtesy of The Anne and Michael Spalter Digital Art Collection.

img.credit: Spalter Digital. 2023. Return To Square (No. 1 in the Metamorphoses Series). spalterdigital.com

body: The event that legitimized the use of technology in art, Artist Robert Rauschenberg and engineer Billy Klüver (Bell Labs) organized 9 Evenings to promote artist-engineer collaboration. In just eighteen months, Bell Labs engineers went from experimenting with computer art and showcasing their results in a small gallery without much fanfare (Howard Wise) to this large-scale event at one of New York’s most prestigious spaces. In fact, New York City’s 69th Regiment Armory was home to one of the most famous exhibition in North American history, the 1913 Armory Show, which first introduced modern art to America. It was the first large-scale collaboration between artists, engineers and scientists. 30 engineers and 10 artists staged a series of elaborate interdisciplinary performances. They realized work that would have been unachievable on their own. The artists used state-of-the-art technology such as computers, video cameras, and projectors to create their works. This marked a significant departure from traditional forms of art-making and opened up future possibilities for artists to experiment with technology. The show featured some of the most intrepid artists of the day including Deborah Hay, Lucinda Childs and John Cage. It also increased the awareness of technology’s use in art in the broader artist community. Besides the immense legacy of the show itself, 9 Evenings also directly led to Rauschenberg and Klüver forming Experiments in Art and Technology (EAT). EAT, further promoting artist-engineer collaboration, would change the use of technology to make art irrevocably.

img.credit: Wikipedia. 2023. "9 Evenings: Theatre and Engineering." Wikimedia Foundation. Last modified July 3, 2023. en.wikipedia.org.

body: Arranged by the Western Association of Art Museums, the show featured Mason’s analog computer work, much of it would later be included in Cybernetic Serendipity.
The American Mason had a background in the military as well as computer science, working at IBM in Silicon Valley for decades.
His contributions to computer art are less often noted today but a deeper dive into the mercurial artist’s work remains rewarding.
Image is copyrighted by Maughan S. Mason and courtesy of The Anne and Michael Spalter Digital Art Collection.

body: The early natural language processing (NLP) computer program ELIZA is published by Joseph Weizenbaum, a computer scientist and MIT professor. Named after the protagonist in George Bernard Shaw’s Pygmalion, ELIZA is a forerunner of subsequent chatbots, using pattern matching rules to engage humans in conversation. -Sasha Stiles

Having studied with the poet M.C. Richards and composer John Cage at Black Mountain College, artist Stan VanDerBeek begins developing Poemfields, a series of eight computer-generated films that introduce his “image-based poetry language.” In collaboration with computer scientist Ken Knowlton at Bell Labs, VanDerBeek uses Knowlton’s BEFLIX and an IBM 7094 from 1966-1971.
-Sasha Stiles
Casey Reas also mentions Poemfields to Le Random as an important early generative film that played a role dematerializing art.
Listen to Peter Bauman’s interview with A. Michael Noll (transcript) where he discusses Knowlton, BEFLIX and the early days at Bell Labs.
*Image credit: The Stan VanDerBeek Archive. Courtesy of the artist

First published in French in 1958, and drawing from Claude Shannon’s Information Theory as well as George David Birkhoff, Moles aimed to use techniques of information theory to analyze art. In other words, he sought to view art as communication and analyze it like a science. He developed these theories independently from Max Bense despite both having the aim to of using scientific means to understand aesthetics. Philip Galanter argues that the work of Bense and Moles was instrumental in the early development of complexity science and aesthetics. Moles, for example explored statistical measures of musical order and disorder, valuing it from “banal” to “novel” in an early attempt to understand the relationship between complexity and aesthetics.

img.credit: Abraham Moles. Information Theory and Esthetic Perception. 1966.

body: Nake won the first prize of the 1966 Computers and Automation contest with an untitled drawing of small squares, recorded by Compart as Zufällige Zeichenverteilung (1965). Nake then wrote about his other significant 1966 work, Walk-Through-Raster (plotter drawings). Underscoring the importance of mathematics in his work, Nake wrote about Walk-Through-Raster:
“The secrets behind algorithmic art can really be fathomed only when we allow for mathematical descriptions.”
Nake used the ALGOL 60 programming language and the Z64 Graphomat plotter.

body: The exhibition was the first in the United States to showcase the emerging Minimalism movement, presenting simplified geometric sculptures made with colorful, industrial materials. It was curated by Kynaston McShine who would go on to curate Information at MoMA in 1970.

body: According to Art Historian Frank Popper, this exhibition was “one of the founding moments of technological art.” Featuring work from Man Ray, László Moholy-Nagy and others, the exhibition showcased the use of light in contemporary art and sculpture. It was an important step in the development of digital art. It was shown at Stedelijk van Abbemuseum in Eindhoven, Holland.

body: The work by Victor Vasarely’s son, part of a series, was made of cord, steel and wood to create the illusion of pulsation and dynamism. The GRAV member Yvaral “created a link from his early optical research and his interest in science as a model for artistic creation with a subtle use of the computer for the programming of a pictorial surface,” according to Art Historian Frank Popper. The work is an important example of the link between New Tendencies, in particular GRAV.

body: Founded by engineers Billy Klüver and Fred Waldhauer and artists Robert Rauschenberg and Robert Whitman, following the success of their 9 Evenings show, the aim of Experiments in Art and Technology (EAT) was to promote collaboration between engineers and artists. The group would prove to be one of the most influential and important in computer art history. The first meeting was held in November 1966. EAT News, a newsletter featuring short articles, began the following year. The group formed after the successful 9 Evenings show earlier in the year.

img.cap: The front page of E.A.T. News vol. 1 no. 2 (1 June 1967), setting out the purpose of Experiments in Art and Technology beneath its masthead and signed by Billy Klüver and Robert Rauschenberg.

body: This exhibition at the Deutsche Rechenzentrum (German Computing Center) in Darmstadt featured computer music, drawings and text. It helped to popularize computer art in Germany and beyond. It’s also important showing of several (~21) early Frieder Nake works. Released with the exhibition was “Programm-Information Pl-21” a booklet that was one of the first publications explicitly dedicated to computer art and included an essay by Nake on computer graphics.

body: Having collaborated with the likes of John Cage and Marcel Duchamp, Fluxus poet Alison Knowles teams up with composer James Tenney to write The House of Dust – one of the earliest computer-generated poems, dated 1966 to 1968 by ZKM. The text begins as a set of four lists written by Knowles, which are then generated into quatrains via a program written by Tenney using FORTRAN on an IBM computer.
-Sasha Stiles

body: Following its first meeting in November 1966, EAT held its press launch at co-founder Robert Rauschenberg’s Manhattan studio. The meeting was attended by a variety of artists and engineers (from IBM and Bell Labs). EAT would go on to play an instrumental role in popularizing computer art and promoting technology and art, building upon their seminal 1966 exhibition, 9 Evenings.

body: In his essay “Paragraphs on Conceptual Art,” LeWitt fixed the term in art-world usage, famously writing that “the idea becomes a machine that makes the art.”
LeWitt continued: “I will refer to the kind of art in which I am involved as conceptual art. In conceptual art the idea of concept is the most important aspect of the work.”

img.credit: Wikipedia. 2023. "Sol LeWitt." Wikimedia Foundation. Last modified September 6, 2023. en.wikipedia.org.

body: After a decade in painting and then years at The Ohio State University making analogue computer drawings, Charles Csuri finally got his hands on a digital computer for art making in 1967. His practice exploded onto the computer art scene that year with several key works.

First was his piece with James Shaffer, Sine Curve Man, which was the Computers and Automation first prize winner for 1967. Csuri would also produce the seminal plotter drawings Random War and Aging Process in 1967. Random War would go on to be shown at Jasia Reichardt's Cybernetic Serendipity the following year.

Sine Curve Man began as a line drawing of a man. Csuri and Shaffer, of Ohio State’s mathematics department, reshaped it with a sine curve function on an IBM mainframe and drew the stages on a plotter, since they had no way yet to record it as animation.

Csuri's experience reminds me of many people who already had a creative dam filling that was ready to burst once they got access to the right tooling. A contemporary example would be Ryan Murdock, who explained to me how his work with CLIP and GANs was already anticipated by his prior work. He just needed the CLIP part. Csuri, like Molnár around this same time, just needed access to digital computation.

img.cap: https://spalterdigital.com/artworks/sine-curve-man-2/
img.credit: Spalter Digital. 2023. Sine Curve Man. spalterdigital.com

body: One of the earliest computer animations, Csuri moved away from the geometric abstraction of his European computer art peers, introducing figuration to computer art.
Csuri generated more than 14,000 frames in which the bird is exploded, scattered and put back together, outputting them to 16mm film.

Csuri’s figurative work highlights the breadth of computer art’s capabilities, showing the world a computer could produce more than the abstract visualization of mathematical formulae. This piece is in the MoMA permanent collection and is one of the earliest computer-generated works to enter its collection.

body: This work, from Nees’s series exploring the polygon from 1965-1968, investigates the relationship between “order and complexity” and "aesthetic measure.”
These concepts were developed by Abraham Moles and Max Bense in Europe, drawing on George David Birkhoff’s aesthetic measure and on Claude Shannon’s information theory at Bell Labs.

body: This piece by the pioneer computer artist Robbins celebrates the intricacy of geometric forms and their ability to capture nature’s inner beauty. Robbins describes the piece: “This five-pointed star is a three-pointed star, used to check out the incremental step on an incremental plotter, superimposed upon itself. The design has many straight lines at many differnt angles. It was produced on a large Gerber flatbed plotter.” Robbins would go on to be included at Cybernetic Serendipity the following year.
This colored plotter drawing features four squares with algorithmically assigned colors. An edition of this series is included in the Victoria and Albert Museum.
Nake produced the series on a Telefunken TR 4 computer between 1967 and 1968.

body: Created by Harmon and Knowlton at Bell Labs, this computer generated photomural of a reclining nude, twelve feet long, was made entirely of abstract symbols.

Consisting of bitmapped ASCII characters, Computer Nude is one of the most famous and recognizable of the early computer artworks and is one of the first ASCII artworks. Harmon and Knowlton had been introduced by Experiments in Art and Technology (EAT).

In the collection of the Buffalo AKG Art Museum, the piece “demonstrates the unique capacity of the viewer’s brain to interpret a composition of abstract symbols grouped to emulate areas of tonal value as a human figure.” The piece would be exhibited the following year at the legendary The machine, as seen at the end of the mechanical age.

body: The Center was established at The Massachusetts Institute of Technology (MIT) by Kepes “to bring artists from around the world to collaborate with MIT’s community of scientists and engineers, [in order] to produce works using new directions in technological approach.” It was attempted to create a community of innovators, providing opportunities for artists such as Nam June Paik and Stan Vanderbeek. Over the course of 42 years, more than 200 artists would go through CAVS. This interdisciplinary center was MIT’s first foray into contemporary art and an important step in the development of MIT as a critical interlocutor between art and science.

body: Designed by Wally Feurzeig, Seymour Papert and Cynthia Solomon, Logo was a general purpose programming language that was hugely important to the development of computer art. It’s main innovation for computer graphics was the concept of “turtle graphics,” allowing a programmer to manipulate the movement of a robotic turtle sitting on the floor. After being further developed at MIT in the 1970s, Logo would play an instrumental role in the development of generative art again in the 1980s as the language was taught in public schools, influencing a new generation of creative coders and artists, such as Casey Reas.

img.credit: Wikipedia. 2023. "Logo (programming language)." Wikimedia Foundation. Last modified June 12, 2023. en.wikipedia.org).

body: This iconic early computer-generated drawing features squares on a grid that become increasingly disordered from top to bottom, exploring what would become a central theme in computer generative art, the relationship between order and disorder.

img.cap: Georg Nees's Schotter, the plotter drawing in which a grid of squares slips row by row out of alignment, from order at the top into scattered disorder at the bottom.
img.credit: Georg Nees, Schotter. (c) Victoria and Albert Museum, London.

body: Cybernetic Serendipity, Jasia Reichardt’s landmark international exhibition at the Institute of Contemporary Arts, London, ran from 2 August to 20 October 1968 and was computer art’s first international exhibition. But it was also so much more than that.

With cybernetic theory (Cybernetics Is Born) as an overarching theme, the exhibition probed the relationship between creativity and technology. It “aroused world-wide interest for computer art and especially for computer graphics,” according to Herbert Franke. It accomplished this by comprehensively showcasing the various movements’ pioneers.

The show featured pioneers in a staggering variety of digital arts, including A. Michael Noll, Frieder Nake, Georg Nees, CTG and Charles Csuri (computer graphics), Nam June Paik (video art), Jean Tinguely (kinetic art), John Cage (generative music), Jeanne Beaman (generative choreography), John Whitney (computer film), Ken Knowlton (computer animation) and many others.

Cybernetic Serendipity was forward looking, it “deal[t] with possibilities rather than achievements,” according to Reichardt. The genius of the exhibition is that several decades later the collective achievements of the artists at the exhibition are innumerable.

The publication itself is even a prized possession today and a work of art. Reichardt said that “the most important single revelation of this exhibition” was that, due to the advent of computers, “people who would never have put pencil to paper, or brush to canvas, have started making images.”

This is the legacy of Cybernetic Serendipity. Its promotion of art and technology inspired experimentation and collaboration in the arts that are still reverberating today. It established the computer as an integral force in the history of art, inspired numerous pioneers and introduced cybernetic art to a global audience.
From Cybernetics Is Born:

Cybernetics would play a vital role in both the birth of digital art and artificial intelligence, thus making it one of the single most important moments on the timeline. Max Bense and his role at the University of Stuttgart explains the connection to computer art, specifically. He taught the first European computer artists, Georg Nees and Frieder Nake, leaving an indelible marks on their thinking that last to this day, as youtube.com demonstrates.

For artificial intelligence, cybernetics was an early attempt to unite machines and organic beings in a functional way, as it sought a theory of control, feedback and communication applicable to machines as well as animals. In the book Art in the Age of Machine Learning, author Sofian Audry argues that the concept of machine learning dates back to cybernetics.

body: The iconic exhibition inspired Software and facilitated art’s transition from the mechanical to the digital. Curated by collector and museum director, K.G. Pontus Hultén, the exhibition aimed to put the intersection of art and technology into historical perspective. Hultén wanted to examine the human-machine relationship with an extensive art historical overview. The detailed exhibition included over 200 pieces by more than 100 artists from the Renaissance to 1968. Artists ranged from Dürer and da Vinci to Tinguely and Tatlin. It traced the development of the myriad ways artists related to technology over time. From our mechanical past to the newly digitizing 1968, the exhibition questioned the consequences of these changes. “The Machine” also featured contemporary artists at the forefront of digital computing and art. Leon D. Harmon and Ken Knowlton of Bell Labs exhibited their celebrated early computer graphic, Studies in Perception I. Robert Rauschenberg, John Cage and Billy Klüver of Experiments in Art and Technology (EAT) exhibited nine works from a world-wide competition. The winner was Jean Dupuy’s “Heart Beats Dust.” Art historian Frank Popper called the show "a significant early moment in the passage from the mechanical to the electronic age in art.” It examined humanity’s mechanical past, opening the door for future artists to ask the new, difficult questions facing humans and technology.

body: Gottfried Jäger, Hein Gravenhorst, Kilian Breier and Pierre Cordier introduced the art world to the concept of generative photography with this eponymous exhibit at Bielefeld Kunsthaus. Rather than thinking about photography as a mirror of the real world, Jäger’s generative photography was non-representational. This abstract work showcased the creative, yet scientific, experimentation possible with the device. According to art critic Georg Bak: “Photomechanical transformations, chemigrams, luminograms and pinhole structures presented a non-representational, systematic-constructive photographic visual language.” While an important movement in its own right, generative photography also served as critical stepping stone in the digitization of art. Herbert Franke explains how the generative processes used by Gravenhorst and Jäger “are results of a generative photography created in programmed working stages. From here it is but a step to electronic automation and so to the computer.”

body: The Hungarian theoretical biologist and botanist, Lindenmayer, developed Lindenmayer systems (or L-systems) to mathematically describe the growth processes of plant development.

This algorithmic botany is still used today by artists such as Zancan and Johnathan McCabe in digital generative art to mimc the fractal patterns of trees and plants. In fact, Le Random’s collection has two excellent contemporary examples that highlight the algorithm: McCabe’s Evotree #1 (2023) and Zancan’s Lushtemples — Highlights of the Hike.

Engelbart’s presentation included demos of the mouse, word processing, the first graphical user interface (UGI), hypertext, video conferencing, real-time collaboration, and other modern computing concepts. body: In an attempt to make graphic design on computers more accessible to those without programming experience, Mezei developed the early computer graphics language SPARTA in 1968. SPARTA, a Procedure Oriented Programming for the Manipulation Language of Arbitrary Line Drawings consisted of “FORTRAN libraries of programs featuring graphic primitives and transformations like lines, polygons, rotation, and translation, and more sophisticated transformations, including a random number generator.”

body: Founded by kinetic artist and astronautical pioneer Frank Malina in Paris, the importance and relevance of Leonardo to this day cannot be overstated. It aimed “to serve as an international channel of communication among artists, with emphasis on the writings of artists who use science and developing technologies in their work.” Leonardo was published by Pergamon Press from 1968 to 1991 and has been published by the MIT Press since. It appears six times a year and continues today. For nearly 60 years it has played a an out-sized role in popularizing and promulgating insights and developments in the application of the arts on science and technology.

body: CAyC played an important role in the development of Systems art and Conceptual art in Latin America. It was led by Jorge Glusberg from its 1968 founding, as CEAC, until his death in 2012. CAyC was a space for artists to exhibit their work as well as “a multidisciplinary workshop to explore the relationship between art, science and social studies; it positioned itself as a space to generate a new wave of experimental art.” From the Bright Moments Buenos Aires Timeline Poster: Jorge Glusberg established the Centro de Arte y Comunicación (CAyC) in Buenos Aires. CAyC served as a multidisciplinary artist workshop, fostering an innovative space where artists converged to explore the intersection of art, science and communication. The concept of “systems” served as the central framework linking CAyC’s diverse endeavors.

body: Founded by Alan Sutcliffe, George Mallen and John Lansdown, the Society (1968-1985) was formed “to encourage the creative use of computers and to allow the exchange of information in this area.” For decades CAS has aimed to advance the understanding of digital and electronic media’s role in the arts. It was initially founded in ‘68 by Alan Sutcliffe, George Mallen and John Lansdown after advising and participating in Cybernetic Serendipity. The original version would run until 1985. It experienced a renaissance in between 2002 and 2004 and continues to this day (2024). Dedicated to fostering creative computer use, it preserves the rich history of computer-generated art and is now even part of the Victoria and Albert Museum’s collections. As of 2024, CAS continues to promote digital media in contemporary practice, hosts events, exhibitions and an annual Electronic Visualisation & the Arts (EVA) conference.

body: This show by Computer Technique Group (CTG) was held at the Tokyo Gallery, Ginza Miyuki Avenue. The group exhibited Automatic Painting Machine No 1 for the first time, which helped to garner public attention in Japan and elsewhere for their work. Critic and Cybernetic Serendipity curator Jasia Reichardt “recognized that the images produced by CTG were not only different from those produced elsewhere, but were the “most imaginative,” according to Grant Taylor. CTG was seeking to transition the mechanical Lumino-Kinetic, participative art of the previous years, especially that of the Gutai group to the digital.

body: The Snail by Kerry Strand, and Symplexity by Kerry Strand and Larry Jenkins, were important early computer-generated drawings for their curvilinear forms.

These more organic forms were in contrast to the mostly rectilinear compositions of the time. Grant Taylor explains: “The Snail and other curvilinear figures completed by technologists became precursors to the later 1980s computer art of William Latham and others who abstracted nature’s morphogenetic process and created strange biomorphic forms.”

body: Vera Molnár’s machine imaginaire became a machine réelle in 1968, when she gained access to her first computer through her friend Pierre Barbaud, a French algorithmic composer. Barbaud invited Molnár to the Bull-GE headquarters in Gambetta, where she created the work 1 des premieres images d’après listing – BULL 1968. Molnár generated the piece by having the computer print out numbers corresponding to colors, which she then colored by hand. Molnár would not soon forget this experience, as she would ensure she had regular access to a computer later in the year.

body: Molnár’s earliest computer art phase began in 1968 with a short series of untitled plotter drawings and the open series Interruptions (1968–69).

These early works consisted entirely of rectilinear forms of varying angles, randomly arranged by Molnár’s own algorithm. In her own words from an interview with Hans Ulrich Obrist she describes them:

“They’re square grids, and in each frame there’s either a vertical or a horizontal line, or nothing. 45° and 135°. Four inclines, plus empty space. This you can’t do by hand. It’s the same thing – I still work like that with grids, it’s one of my subjects.”

For Molnár it was both a learning experience and revelation: “I was not very good at programming but I finally understood how to do very simple things, this geometric way of working.” She would describe the beginning of her work with computers to Obrist as well:

“The real, actual computer was in 1968. That I remember really well. In 1968 we thought that everything was possible and all you have to do is knock on the doors and the doors open. So, armed with this certainty, I went and knocked at the door of the Paris University computing centre, which was in Orsay, and I explained to the head of the centre that I wanted to try to make art with a computer.

He gave me a look and I had the feeling that he was considering whether he should call for a nurse to sedate me or lock me up or something. Later, when I got to know this man, he told me: ‘I said yes to you because I thought of a famous quote by Voltaire, the one where he says: ‘I completely disagree with everything that you are saying but will defend until my death your right to do or say or write what you have in mind’’, and so he said yes.

That was easily said, it was an honour for me, but I had no privileges whatsoever because it was for scientists and researchers: I was nothing in all that. Back then, it was very expensive, we had to rent computers by the minute, so I sort of shrunk in a corner, the last in line, but I was still there.”

body: The former Artforum editor played a key role in advancing the role of technology in art. His writings, including this book, also explain in great details the dematerialization of sculpture occuring, an important step in the advancement of digital art and electronic art. In the prescient book, Burnham outlines the historical transition from sculpture-as-object to sculpture-as-system, driven by technology. Sculpture-as-system included automata, kineticism, light and cybernetic. Burnham explores the historical roots of these movements, including the importance of New Tendencies and Cybernetics. According to Burnham, “change emanates not from things but from the way things are done.”

“That thesis was soon widely consulted by the small but growing community, harnessing the words generative and computer together in its readers’ minds.”
One of the first book-length publications on computer art, this doctoral dissertation, completed with the guidance of Max Bense, was completed in 1968 and published in 1969.

Leicester Polytechnic would for nearly a decade and a half become one of the most important centers of computer art in Britain and the world.

body: The Venezuelan kinetic art pioneer sought to involve the viewer physically with his immense and immersive Pénétrables installations. These large works consisted of thousands of strands, hanging from above, encouraging viewers to physically interact with the work. body: This New Tendencies magazine published by Zagreb City Galleries would release nine editions from 1968-1972.

The Zagreb group would go on to organize the iconic Tendencies 4 in 1969. 1968 saw the release of “Bit No. 1: The Theory of Information and the New Aesthetics,” which closely examined the thoughts of Max Bense and Abraham Moles.

“Bit No. 2: Computers and Visual Research” was also released in 1968 and featured the writings of A. Michael Noll, Herbert Franke, Hiroshi Kawano, Georg Nees, Frieder Nake and Leslie Mezei among others. The magazine serves a critical link between the New Tendencies movement and computer-generated art.
