body: From November 26, 1968, to January 5, 1969, the Brooklyn Museum hosted Some More Beginnings, an exhibition presented by Experiments in Art and Technology (E.A.T.). Shown in conjunction with MoMA’s The Machine as Seen at the End of the Mechanical Age. The previous year, E.A.T. announced a competition—aiming to spur collaboration between artists and engineers—with the best work being feature in MoMA’s The Machine. Nine works ended up being included, while the remaining 137 were shown at the Brooklyn Museum in Some More Beginnings. The nine works shown with The Machine include works by Jean Dupuy, Tsai Wen-Ying, Lucy Jackson Young, Hilary Harris, Lillian Schwartz, Robin Parkinson, Leon D. Harmon and John William Anthes. The work included cybernetic and interactive pieces that spoke, moved, and engaged viewers in new ways. The exhibition marked yet another demonstration of the widespread interest these interventions with emerging technologies elicited in the late 1960s.

body: Begun in 1968 and continuing until his death in 2007, LeWitt’s seminal Wall Drawings were important examples of randomness in systems-based art. These instruction-based works of conceptual installation art also challenged the notions of authorship and permanence as LeWitt made the instructions for the drawings yet did not necessarily execute them himself.

body: Published in Computers and Automation, the brief article by Tsuchiya stresses the importance of process, randomness and system in computer art. It asks finally, “Can the computer art that is a hobby of engineers and automatically-made art become a new world of aesthetics?” Tsuchiya suggests that the “secrets of wonderful works” can be found in the “balance of system and randomness that computer art provides.”

body: Tendencies 4: Computers and Visual Research was a groundbreaking exhibition held at the Gallery of Contemporary Art, Zagreb, today the Museum of Contemporary Art, showcasing the convergence of art and digital technology. It featured the latest computer graphics and computer-programmed work of the time, featuring prominent artists such as Frieder Nake, Georg Nees and A. Michael Noll.

The previous three Tencencies exhibitions earlier in the ’60s focused on op art, cybernetic art and lumino-kinetic sculpture, highlighting the importance of those movements in the genealogy of computer art and digital generative art.

By Tendencies 4 in 1969, the focus had shifted away from the material and toward the digital, spurring the dematerialization of art. Tendencies 4 showcased computer-generated graphics, information theory and conceptual works.

body: The Advanced Research Projects Agency Network (ARPANET), precursor to the modern Internet, went live in September 1969, with four host computers connected by year’s end. ARPANET’s development facilitated the exchange of information and ideas among scientists and researchers, creating a fertile environment for artistic experimentation in the coming decades.

body: The landmark exhibition and symposium held at the Sogetsu Hall in Tokyo featured Kinetic, Light, and Lumino-Kinetic works from Japan, Western Europe and North America. Its installations utilized the tools of mass media including lasers, UV, strobe lights, TVs and various other electronics. Computer Technique Group (CTG) exhibited their works Thermo Field (a thermal painting machine) and Plotting Field. For Plotting Field, the group used a CalComp plotter to produce iterations of their John F. Kennedy images. Besides CTG, several other prominent artists participated in the exhibition. Katsuhiro Yamaguchi showed his Image Modulator made from a TV and glass. Nicholas Schöffer exhibited Chrons 8, a two-meter high steel and light, mechanized sculpture. Finally, Minoru Yoshida of the Gutai group exhibited the cybernetic, mechanized sculpture, EP3. This exhibition further demonstrates the connection between Lumino-Kinetic Art and computer art, as well as the international nature of the movement.

body: Inspired by Constructivism, Jeffrey Steele, a former Op Art painter, founded the Systems group, which included artists such as John Ernest, Gillian Wise and Malcolm Hughes. Their work, which was anchored in postwar mathematics and cybernetics, investigated the increasing scale and complexity of systems, raising concerns about the visibility of underlying systems in the finished artwork. As technology improved, artists such as Steele and John Ernest adopted a materialist and generative art technique that celebrated chance and disturbed systems. The group’s goal was to investigate the productive capacities of systems other than humans, arguing for self-sufficient systems. Questions though developed about the potential alienation of systems from the artist, sparking arguments about the role of predefined and changing systems in artistic expression. In 1973, Malcolm Hughes would go on to found the Computer and Experimental Department at the University College London’s Slade School of Art, an important UK computer art hub. Artists such as Paul Brown, Stephen Bell, Stephen Scrivener and Dominic Boreham.

body: Sonakinatography is the breakthrough series by Horwitz, meaning “sound,” “motion” and “notation.” On graph paper, she plotted the motion of eight entities over time with colors and numbers in 8x8 square grids. This work highlights the relationship between artists, technology and machines.

body: At the end of 1969 the group decided to disband citing difficulties collaborating with each other. According to Grant Taylor, “Haruki Tsuchiya said that the collaborative effort had not been as easy as expected and that ultimately artists and technologists are essentially different.” The end of the ’60s saw interest in technology and art peak before quieting down in the ’70s. The dissolution of CTG was indicative of this sentiment reversal. The group’s legacy remains immense, as CTG can be seen as the first modern digital generative artists for thinking of their work in terms of art-making systems. Grant Taylor explains their defining impact: “Most importantly, though, CTG was the first to envisage the artist as a constructor of a system—a system that would create large amounts of form rather than individual artworks.”

img.cap: CTG's APM (Automatic Painting Machine) No. 1 of 1968, a four-colour spray gun on an X-Y arm driven by its own logic unit — the group's clearest statement of the artist as builder of a form-making system.
img.credit: Computer Technique Group (CTG), APM (Automatic Painting Machine) No. 1, 1968. Image: compArt database of digital art (dada), University of Bremen.

body: Leicester Polytechnic is designated in April 1969, formed by the merger of Leicester School of Art and Leicester Technical College. Stroud Cornock and Ernest Edmonds become influential figures in the international computer art scene, emphasizing the intersection of art and technology. The school’s impact can still be felt today with its legacy alive through the Computer Arts Society where Edmonds is still active. Throughout the decade of the ’70s until the mid-80s, Leicester Polytechnic (eventually the HCIRU Research Group) would attract some of the brightest minds interested in the intersection of art and technology, including Stephen Scrivener and then Dominic Boreham.

body: ADALINE (Adaptive Linear Neuron or Element) was a foundational single-layer artificial neural network. But don't be fooled into thinking it was simple, as it was surprisingly modern. Its architecture had inputs, weights and bias; its learning rule, Least Mean Squares (LMS) algorithm, was even based on stochastic gradient descent.
Where Rosenblatt's Perceptron (see earlier on the timeline) learned only from a right-or-wrong verdict, ADALINE learned from how far off its score was before the yes/no call was made.
Electrical engineer Bernard Widrow and his first graduate student, Marcian “Ted” Hoff created ADALINE at Stanford University, describing it in their 1960 paper “Adaptive Switching Circuits.”

The lunch-pail-sized machine read crude letter patterns set on a four-by-four grid of toggle switches and learned to sort them. After each example, all 17 of its weights moved by equal amounts to bring the error to zero. This is the famous LMS rule mentioned above, following the error downhill one example at a time. To this day, the Smithsonian holds two ADALINEs.

img.cap: Bernard Widrow with one of the ADALINE machines he built with Ted Hoff.
img.credit: Bernard Widrow with an ADALINE machine, about 1963. Via Wikimedia Commons.

body: In 1967, Japanese engineer Shun-ichi Amari published “A Theory of Adaptive Pattern Classifiers” in IEEE Transactions on Electronic Computers.

The paper described learning by nudging a machine’s weights after each example, the canonical method known as stochastic gradient descent. Jürgen Schmidhuber calls it probably the first paper to use the method for learning in multilayer neural networks.

Amari trained a five-layer network to sort patterns that no single straight boundary could separate. In 1972 he published a network that learned to associate patterns by changing its connection weights. John Hopfield’s much more well known 1982 network rests on the same basic equations and is sometimes called the Amari-Hopfield network.

img.cap: A portrait of Shun-ichi Amari, Professor Emeritus of the University of Tokyo, in 2019.
img.credit: Shun’ichi Amari, 2019. CC BY 4.0, via Wikimedia Commons.

body: Much of this Timeline's history of AI will focus on the cybernetic-connectionist-deep learning thread. However, we will from time to time highlight major advancements in symbolic, expert systems. One of the earliest hard-coded AI expert systems used for scientific reasoning was DENDRAL.

In 1965 at Stanford University, computer scientist Edward Feigenbaum asked Nobel laureate Joshua Lederberg for a scientific problem to study hypothesis formation. Lederberg, involved in NASA’s search for life on Mars, suggested identifying unknown molecules from mass spectrometry data.

And they did and they created DENDRAL, a program that generated every chemically valid arrangement of a molecule’s atoms and pruned the list with chemists’ "expert" rules of thumb. The team asked chemist Carl Djerassi, “What do you know about this problem that the program does not know?” Bruce Buchanan and Georgia Sutherland turned the answers into rules, working with Djerassi’s colleague Alan Duffield.
It was precisely this kind of expert system that would gain in popularity in the '70s and '80s while neural network AI experienced a prolonged winter.

img.cap: Joshua Lederberg at work in his laboratory in 1958, a few years before he and Edward Feigenbaum began DENDRAL.
img.credit: Joshua Lederberg in his laboratory at the University of Wisconsin, October 1958. Via Wikimedia Commons.

body: In 1962 Viktor Glushkov, director of the Institute of Cybernetics in Kyiv, proposed OGAS with Anatoly Kitov and others, a nationwide computer network to manage the Soviet command economy. At its most ambitious, up to twenty thousand computer centers were planned to feed several hundred regional centers and one center in Moscow.
Glushkov imagined OGAS, as a “brainlike” network. But the project would stall in bureaucratic limbo for nearly a decade.

It reached the Politburo on October 1, 1970, a year after ARPANET went online. The 1971 Party Congress even approved the network and 1,600 factory control systems but OGAS was stripped of its more experimental design, becoming a purely technical network.

body: For ages, it was easy to imagine and fear but impossibly difficult to concretely understand the capabilities of an "ultraintelligent machine" or what the ramifications would be for humanity, if we did indeed make one. Back in the 1950s and '60s, statistician I. J. Good all too presciently did the imagining part.

In 1965, Good, who had worked with Alan Turing at Bletchley Park, published “Speculations Concerning the First Ultraintelligent Machine” in Advances in Computers. Such a machine, able to far surpass the intellectual activities of any person, could also design better machines, setting off what Good called an intelligence explosion. “The first ultraintelligent machine is the last invention that man need ever make,” he wrote, provided it told humans how to keep it under control.

Good also consulted on Stanley Kubrick’s 2001: A Space Odyssey, whose shipboard computer HAL kills most of the crew. Personally, I find it comforting to find contemporary fears perfectly mirrored in decades past. It defangs our current fears a bit, or perhaps only confirms them.
Jasia Reichardt, writing for Le Random, wrote about Good and the ultraintelligent machine: “The Ultraintelligent Machine and Gaberbocchus Common Room”.

img.cap: A replica of HAL 9000, the shipboard computer of 2001: A Space Odyssey, on which Good consulted.
img.credit: Replica of HAL 9000 from 2001: A Space Odyssey. Via Wikimedia Commons.

body: The story of deep learning's ascendance in AI research over decades is a long and twisting tale. But it's remarkable how quickly its theory and potential were recognized.

In their 1965 book Cybernetic Predicting Devices, Soviet scientists Alexey Ivakhnenko and Valentin Lapa set out a way to train networks with many layers. The approach, known as the Group Method of Data Handling (GMDH), grew a network one layer at a time. Each unit fitted a simple curve to its inputs and any unit that did poorly on fresh test data was dropped. Ivakhnenko likened it to plant breeding.

In 1971, at the Institute of Cybernetics in Kyiv, Ivakhnenko described a GMDH network eight layers deep. Jürgen Schmidhuber’s 2015 survey of deep learning calls such networks “perhaps the first” deep learning systems of the multilayer perceptron type. No big deal.

img.cap: A portrait of Alexey Ivakhnenko.
img.credit: Alexey Ivakhnenko. CC BY-SA 4.0, via Wikimedia Commons.

body: In October 1966, a pattern recognition committee of the Institute of Electrical and Electronics Engineers (IEEE) held the first Pattern Recognition Workshop in Dorado, Puerto Rico. A second met in Delft, the Netherlands, in August 1968.

The workshops served researchers applying neural networks and statistical methods to pattern recognition, speech and computer vision, approaches that Nils Nilsson notes came to be called “nonsymbolic” to set them apart from symbol-processing (expert system) AI. Later, this "nonsymbolic" or learning approach would be called connectionism; finally, it would be called deep learning.

The committee became the IEEE’s Technical Committee on Pattern Analysis and Machine Intelligence, which now sponsors the CVPR computer vision conference. Read about Luba Elliott's curation of the CVPR 2026 Art Gallery in “Seeing Machines: Luba Elliott on the 2026 CVPR Art Gallery”.

body: Easily one of the most important and (in)famous moments in AI history, the moment when the field essentially was split in two. This division would last for decades and greatly impact the opposing side of learning almost irreparably. Into the 2000s, researchers in the symbolic camp would still cite (very mistakenly) Marvin Minsky for why neural nets would never work. Well this is the reason. By 2010, the learning side had all but won. By the second quarter of this century, deep learning, a direct descendant of Rosenblatt's perceptron, would be king.
Marvin Minsky and Seymour Papert’s Perceptrons (1969) entrenched the two artificial intelligence traditions, by seemingly disproving the learning side and Rosenblatt's perceptron.

Minsky and Papert backed symbolic AI's programs based on logical rules. Rosenblatt's learning tradition built networks that adjusted their connections from examples, whose limits the book set out in mathematical proofs. Those proofs were read as showing that neural networks had no future, and the Nobel Committee for Physics writes that the book “led to a hiatus funding-wise” for neural network research.

Sociologist Mikel Olazaran traces that reading to symbolic AI’s rise and its control of resources and authority. When neural networks revived in the late 1980s, the official history was rewritten. Yes, it would take two decades before anyone, especially in the West, took neural nets seriously again.

img.cap: A diagram of the Mark I Perceptron from its 1960 operator’s manual: the kind of learning machine Perceptrons was read as ruling out.
img.credit: Mark I Perceptron, figure 2 of its operator’s manual, 1960. Via Wikimedia Commons.

body: Robots that can reason might be the stuff of sci-fi nightmares (and current realities). But in 1966, at their infancy, they seemed much more benign. Shakey the Robot, perhaps the first mobile robot to reason about its actions, looked like a photocopier on wheels and it moved blocks. If anything, it's a bit cute.
Led by neural-network researcher Charles Rosen, a team at the Stanford Research Institute (SRI) spent six years building Shakey from 1966 to 1972.

Rosen's team consisted of Nils Nilsson, Bertram Raphael and Peter Hart (who later led it), with Richard Duda, Richard Fikes and Helen Chan Wolf. Guided by a video camera and a remote mainframe, Shakey took instructions in ordinary English and pushed blocks between rooms.
To plan its routes, Hart, Nilsson and Raphael devised the A* search algorithm, published in 1968 and still used to this day to steer characters in video games.

img.credit: Shakey the robot with its parts labeled, SRI International, 1972. CC BY-SA 3.0, via Wikimedia Commons.

body: In 1962 the British mathematician I. J. Good, who had worked with Alan Turing at Bletchley Park, edited The Scientist Speculates: An Anthology of Partly-Baked Ideas for Heinemann in London.

It collected short speculative pieces by scientists on questions they could not yet test, from the nature of mind and consciousness to machine intelligence and life elsewhere in the universe. Good's interest in machines that could improve themselves led three years later to his essay on an “ultraintelligent machine,” an early statement of what is now called the intelligence explosion. The seminal Jasia Reichardt describes the ultraintelligent machine and its story in our Editorials: “The Ultraintelligent Machine and Gaberbocchus Common Room”.

body: Ah, the perceptron, one of the most (in)famous words in AI history. As mentioned previously in this timeline, Frank Rosenblatt first described the Perceptron in 1958.

In 1962 Spartan Books in Washington published Frank Rosenblatt's Principles of Neurodynamics: Perceptrons and the Theory of Brain Mechanisms. This 616-page tome was an account of the perceptron research he had begun at the Cornell Aeronautical Laboratory in 1957.

The book set out the theory and experiments behind networks of simple neuron-like units that learn to classify patterns by adjusting their connections after each error, and it proved that such learning succeeds whenever a solution exists. Rosenblatt also discussed networks with more than one layer of adjustable units, which he could not yet train reliably.

Due to this unreliability in multi-layer perceptrons especially, seven years later in 1969 Minsky and Papert's Perceptrons supposedly disproved the effectiveness of perceptrons and thus neural networks. The impact of this cannot be overstated, as it essentially split the field into connectionism, favoring neural nets and Rosenblatt's perceptron, and symbolism, favoring hard-coded expert systems.

It was the learning versus rules AI split that wouldn't really resolve until around 2010. For decades, neural networks were disavowed and denied funding, largely because "Oh, hadn't they already been disproven by Minsky?"
They weren't and, of course, as you know. The connectionist/perceptron/neural net/Rosenblatt "side" would end up "winning" and is known today as deep learning.

img.credit: Title page of Frank Rosenblatt, Principles of Neurodynamics: Perceptrons and the Theory of Brain Mechanisms (Washington: Spartan Books, 1962). University of Michigan copy, Internet Archive.

body: Embodiments of Mind is a collection of essays and lectures by Warren S. McCulloch and Walter Pitts, the inventors of the neural network (on paper) in 1943.

The book includes that neural network founding paper itself, “A Logical Calculus of the Ideas Immanent in Nervous Activity” (1943), which provided the first mathematical blueprint for artificial neural networks and modern deep learning.

It also includes a 1947 paper on how nervous circuits might recognize the same shape at any size or position. Twenty years after these astronomically important ideas were first formulated, this book helped repopularize the idea of neural networks and perceptrons in AI. This was the era pre-split, before neural networks were disdainfully prejudged (and underfunded) for nearly two decades.

img.cap: The cover of Embodiments of Mind.
img.credit: Cover of Warren S. McCulloch, Embodiments of Mind (Cambridge, MA: MIT Press, 1965). Open Library.

body: Karel Čapek gave us the word "robot" in R.U.R., previously mentioned in this timeline. In 1965 Stanisław Lem published a new book of dire warnings (er, I mean fables).

The book was Cyberiada and its heroes, Trurl and Klapaucius, are rival robot constructors who can build almost anything. In one story Trurl builds the Electronic Bard, a machine that writes poetry on command; asked for a love poem in the language of pure mathematics, it obliges, and its verse drives the kingdom's poets to despair.
These fears have never been hard to imagine. What took sixty years was for fable to connect with theory, technology, data and compute to start turning into reality.

body: Charles “Chuck” Csuri began exploring the possibility of applying computer graphics to art in 1963, while a professor teaching painting at The Ohio State University (OSU).
Originally a painter in the 1950s who canoodled with New York’s avant-garde scene, Csuri became increasingly fascinated with the computer and its potential for art making while at OSU from 1960.

In 1963, he began with analogue "computational" processes with his work After the Artist. He made the work with a device he built to process drawings, working like a pantograph. It changed the length of one or more of its parts, redrawing the traced image in a transformed state.

In 1964 he drew a devil holding a punch card, a jab at the technology of the day. Within three years he was programming a mainframe with the mathematician James Shaffer, where he would produce his most famous early computer art, including Sine Curve Man, Random War and Hummingbird.

body: One of the earliest instances of a digitally modeled sculpture and something approaching 3D printing resulted from Charles Csuri testing a computer's outputs beyond the plotter and film.

For Numeric Milling (1968) one of his collaborators at Ohio State wrote a tool for defining a mathematical surface, the form later known as the Ferguson patch. Csuri had that surface carved in wood on a milling machine in the university’s engineering department. Robert Mallary's Quad III, shown at Cybernetic Serendipity, is another example from this time of computer-generated sculpture.

body: Who is the most referenced historical artist to the code-based generation of today? It may very well be Anni Albers. To this author alone, several artists have mentioned her, including Emily Xie, Tyler Hobbs, Snowfro and Travess. Many likely have a copy of this book on their shelves.

The former Bauhaus weaving workshop student and instructor had moved to the United States in 1933. On Weaving the book treats weaving as a structure of threads crossing at right angles, a grid of binary choices, over or under, from which patterns follow. Obviously "a grid of binary choices" offers a massive clue as to Albers's continued importance if you're reading this from an art and tech, contemporary perspective.

In the book, Albers explained the loom's logic and traced weaving's history from ancient Peru (Ancient Andean Textiles Weave Legacy of Identity), whose textiles she collected, to industrial production. Her analysis of weaving as a system anticipates the view of textiles as a forerunner of computing, from the Jacquard loom onward.

cite.label: Anni Albers. On Weaving. Middletown, CT: Wesleyan University Press, 1965.

body: A rule-based work of art is, simply put, one of the most famous paintings in history, let alone Op Art. In 1961 Bridget Riley painted Movement in Squares, a black-and-white checkerboard whose columns of squares narrow progressively toward one side until the flat surface seems to fold.

The masterpiece is built from a single unit and a strict rule of change, resulting in the appearance of movement and depth in the eye of the viewer. It began the black-and-white works that made Riley a leading figure of Op Art. Her painting Current (1964) would later appear on the catalogue cover of MoMA's exhibition The Responsive Eye in 1965. Today, Movement in Squares is in the Arts Council Collection, London.

cite.label: Bridget Riley, Movement in Squares, 1961. Arts Council Collection, Southbank Centre, London.

body: Have you ever wanted to make sound by drawing?

Daphne Oram did. Oram co-founded the BBC Radiophonic Workshop in 1958 before leaving the following year to work on her own. With a grant from the Calouste Gulbenkian Foundation in 1962 she began building Oramics, a machine that turned drawing into sound.

How exactly in 1962 was this possible you ask? Shapes painted on ten strips of 35 mm film were read by photocells as the strips moved. This controlled a sound's pitch, volume and timbre. It was among the first ways to compose electronic music by drawing, a graphic score that the machine played directly.

body: German artist Hanne Darboven's works of manual systems and numeric thinking in art recall Vera Molnár's machine imaginaire or Charles Csuri's "After Artist" series, pre-computational work that is clearly cognizant of computation.

Working in New York from 1966, Darboven began her Konstruktionen, drawings on graph paper built from systems of numbers. She soon based them on the calendar, adding the digits of each date to produce a sum she then wrote out by hand across page after page.

The results, often filling hundreds of sheets, are records of time counted and written rather than pictures. They are the artifacts of rules and math rather than the divine hand. Darboven worked alongside Sol LeWitt and New York's conceptual art scene, solidifying the connection between rules and conceptualism.

body: Today, interactive work that involves full-body experience is normal, almost expected in contemporary art. But in 1960, participation and interaction were much more radical. A big step in the direction towards more interactive art in the coming decades was the Brazilian artist Lygia Clark's Bichos (Critters), sculptures.

The artworks consisted of flat metal plates joined by hinges that viewers were meant to handle and refold. Each Bicho has many possible configurations and none is considered final: the work is completed by the person moving it. They aren't just conceptually completing the work in the Duchampian sense; they are physically altering the work.
Clark had signed the Neo-Concrete Manifesto in Rio de Janeiro in 1959, which rejected the rigid rationalism of Concrete art for works that involved the body and its fluidity.

cite.label: Lygia Clark: The Abandonment of Art, 1948–1988. The Museum of Modern Art, New York, 2014.

body: The most famous landing in human history was programmed by Margaret Hamilton, who led the team at MIT's Instrumentation Laboratory that wrote the on-board flight software for NASA's Apollo missions.

During the Apollo 11 landing on July 20, 1969, the guidance computer was overloaded with unneeded tasks and raised alarms. Hamilton's team's design, which ran the most important jobs first and dropped the rest, kept the landing on course. Hamilton even promoted and popularized the term “software engineering” to win the discipline the same standing as hardware.
A photograph of her beside a stack of printed code as tall as she is has become an emblem of the work.

cite.label: “Scene at MIT: Margaret Hamilton’s Apollo code.” MIT News, 17 August 2016.

body: Today, it's so common to have a computer in the home we barely notice them. They've become part of the furniture. While the personal computer revolution was still decades away (see the next two chapters), perhaps the first home computer appeared in 1965.

Mary Allen Wilkes, a programmer on the LINC, the small laboratory computer designed at MIT's Lincoln Laboratory, wrote its operating system, LAP6. When the project moved to Washington University in St. Louis, she chose to keep working from her parents' home in Baltimore, where a LINC was installed in the living room.

Wilkes is thus often described as the first person to use a personal computer at home. The LINC itself was extremely influential. Meant for one researcher at a time and operated at a console with a screen and keyboard, the LINC anticipated our desire for computers always nearby.

body: A pioneering work in electronic music, Switched-On Bach consisted of Wendy Carlos, working with the producer Rachel Elkind, playing music by Johann Sebastian Bach on a Moog modular synthesizer, recording each line separately on multitrack tape.
The album showed that an electronic instrument could perform familiar music with precision and character.
It became one of the best-selling classical albums of its time and won three Grammy Awards in 1970. Carlos went on to score Stanley Kubrick's A Clockwork Orange (1971) and Tron (1982).

body: One of the greatest and most referenced works of instruction-based art, Grapefruit remains a canonical example of the dematerialized art object popularized at the time by Lucy Lippard.

Ono published the book on July 4, 1964 in Tokyo, itself consisting of instructions for paintings, music, events and objects, printed in an edition of 500. A work such as “Painting to Be Stepped On” exists as a written instruction that anyone can carry out and each performance of it differs.

While perhaps Ono's most well-known work, the conceptual artist had written instruction pieces since the mid-1950s, which sat close to the early Fluxus event scores of George Brecht and La Monte Young.

Artworks as sets of rules executed by others is the principle that later links conceptual art to code and technological art, as explored in “Living Aesthetics: A Grammar of Protocol Art and Worldbuilding”.

cite.label: Yoko Ono, Grapefruit, Tokyo: Wunternaum Press, 1964. The Museum of Modern Art, New York.
